programme: FOSL1 (Fra-1/AP-1) drives a matrix-degrading, SASP-like inflammatory programme at its targets MMP1, MMP2, MMP9, MMP13, IL6, CXCL8, CCL2 and PLAUR, alongside the AD risk gene CLU, while GRHL2 runs the opposing junctional-maintenance programme at CDH1, CLDN3 and CLDN4 and represses the EMT driver ZEB1 that these same MMPs would otherwise unleash. Together the two factors describe an epithelial/endothelial barrier module tipped toward breakdown by FOSL1 and toward maintenance by GRHL2.
role_in_a: In Alzheimer's disease, FOSL1-driven MMP and cytokine induction is consistent with neurovascular unit and blood-brain barrier breakdown, a well-documented AD feature; the direct FOSL1 target CLU (clusterin) is itself a major AD risk gene tied to amyloid and vascular clearance, and a retrieved paper places FOSL1 in shared endothelial metabolic changes between stroke and AD.
role_in_b: In Huntington's disease no record evidence (no Open Targets association, no publication) places FOSL1 or GRHL2 there; if the module operates in HD it would be by the same generic mechanism — AP-1-driven matrix remodeling overwhelming junctional maintenance in the neurovascular unit — which is documented for HD in the broader literature but not represented in this record.
shared_axis: Both diseases feature progressive neurovascular unit/blood-brain barrier compromise as part of neurodegeneration; a FOSL1-vs-GRHL2 balance between MMP-driven matrix degradation and claudin/cadherin-based junction maintenance is a generic barrier module that could run in either disease's vasculature, even though this record only documents the AD half of that claim.
reasoning: FOSL1 is independently placed in AD by a high Open Targets percentile, two retrieved papers tying it to AD neuroinflammation and endothelial pathology, and a direct target (CLU) that is itself a canonical AD gene; GRHL2 is mechanistically complementary and strongly bound at its targets by ReMap but carries no disease-specific evidence in either condition. Nothing in the record places either factor in HD, so the HD side of the shared axis rests on reasoning about neurovascular biology rather than anything retrieved, which caps this at moderate rather than strong.
support: PMID 39349220 — places FOSL1 in Alzheimer's disease via interleukin-associated neuroprotection signaling; PMID 37775708 — places FOSL1-relevant biology in Alzheimer's disease via shared endothelial metabolic shifts between stroke and AD; no publications found placing FOSL1 or GRHL2 in Huntington's disease.
how_to_falsify: Measure blood-brain barrier permeability markers (e.g. claudin-3/4 protein, MMP1/9 activity) alongside FOSL1 and GRHL2 target expression in matched brain-vascular tissue from AD and HD cohorts (or in AD- and HD-patient iPSC-derived BBB organoids); if FOSL1-target induction and GRHL2-target repression do not track with barrier permeability in HD tissue the way they do in AD tissue, the shared-axis account is wrong.
caveats: Comparison spans blood and brain tissue across 168 patient-group comparisons from 6 independent cohort pairs, so concordance is cross-tissue, not same-cell-type. FOSL1 recurs in 128/168 (76%) and GRHL2 in 121/168 (72%) of comparisons — strong but not universal, and neither is on the single-view or tissue-generic exclusion lists, so the pattern is not an artifact of one subgroup or a generic tissue signal. Critically, neither factor carries any Open Targets association or literature hit for Huntington's disease in this record — the HD half of the story is inferred from vascular biology, not retrieved. Other record evidence points to separate, unincorporated axes (SF1 in hypothalamic HD neurons, UBTF spanning both diseases via ribosomal-transcription literature) that this account does not address.
